newsitem.title: POLAND: Emotions heat up in Poland ahead of May 25 vote.
newsitem.headline: Emotions heat up in Poland ahead of May 25 vote.

text.p: Supporters and opponents of Poland's new draft constitution traded brickbats on Sunday ahead of a May 25 referendum which will decide its fate.
Many priests read out a statement by the country's Roman Catholic bishops urging believers to vote according to their conscience but simultanoeusly stressing the draft's serious moral shortcomings.

In a pastoral letter read out to parishioners in western Kalisz Diocese, Bishop Stanislaw Napierala said the draft, adopted last month by the left-dominated parliament, betrayed basic family values, PAP news agency reported.
A priest in one Warsaw parish urged his flock to vote according to their judgement, but a poster outside the church highlighted attacks on the constitution by leading right-wing politicians.

Poles will be able to approve or reject only the single parliamentary draft in the referendum, because parliament has rejected a proposal to include an alternative drawn up by the right-leaning Solidarity movement.

"If this constitution goes into force, it will mean the loss of Poland's independence and entrench the domination of post-communists," PAP reported one-time Solidarity chaplain Father Henryk Jankowski as telling worshippers.

Opposition to the constitution was also voiced by hundreds of farmers who marched through Warsaw on Sunday to protest against the government's alleged failure to stem the decline of Polish agriculture.

PAP reported Solidarity activists in the southern towns of Rzeszow and Krosno collecting copies of the constitution which they planned to return to sender -- ex-communist President Aleksander Kwasniewski.
Kwasniewski, a strong supporter of the draft co-authored by his former party comrades, had sent copies of the document to every Polish family at the taxpayers' expense.
Parliamentary speaker Jozef Zych, a leader of the co-ruling Peasant Party, voiced support for the draft, calling it the "embodiment of feasible compromise at this point in time."

The constitution was hammered out by the ruling coalition of ex-communists and peasants and two opposition parties: the centrist liberal Union of Freedom (UW) and the left-leaning secularist Labour Union (UP).
Former prime minister Tadeusz Mazowiecki, a leading UW framer of the constitution, angrily reacted to what he called lies by opponents of the draft.
"Poles, do not let yourselves be duped by lies," PAP reported him as telling a UW conference in Warsaw.
"It is untrue that the constitution undermines Poland's sovereignty, wrests children away from their parents and leads to atheism."
He was responding to rightist objections to the draft which would allow Poland to cede some of its prerogatives to international organisations.
The draft's mention of a Children's Rights Spokesman is perceived by rightists as state interference in family affairs, and some of its secular phrasing is viewed as a threat to religion.
But a conference of leading business and industrial associations in the northern city of Olsztyn on Sunday threw its weight behind the draft.

"The constitution adopted by the National Assembly deserves support. Poland needs it for the stability which makes rapid economic growth and the prosperity of citizens possible," PAP reported a resolution passed at the conference as saying.
